subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.textbook_anchor: Clean and Bright — Write down daily activities from waking to sleeping including shower, handwashing, brushing, water intake, eating, sleep, and outdoor play (p. 110)

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites children to share aloud one thing they always do before leaving home in the morning and one thing they always do before sleeping. List responses on the board without comment, letting the variety show.

Students open Textbook p. 110 and read the checklist of daily activities. Each child writes their own full routine in their notebook — from waking up to going to sleep — making sure to include every item from the checklist they actually do.

Children re-read their list and place a tick or a cross next to each habit on the Textbook p. 110 self-check. They notice which habits are already strong and quietly mark one habit they would like to strengthen.

Brief whole-class sharing: children volunteer which habit felt most surprising to examine. Teacher closes by connecting the idea that these habits protect both the body and the mind, framing hygiene as care for oneself.

periods.implied_lo: Students can audit their own daily habits against a health checklist and identify areas for personal improvement.
periods.section_context: Daily hygiene checklist: showering, handwashing with soap, brushing teeth, drinking water, eating, sleeping at least 8 hours, outdoor play; self-audit of brushing twice daily, rinsing after meals, washing hands after toilet and outdoor play.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there any habit on the list that you do every single day without fail — and one that you sometimes forget?' Encourage honest reflection rather than ideal answers; this is a self-check, not a test.

periods.section_ref: How do we Brush our Teeth?
periods.textbook_anchor: How do we Brush our Teeth? — Ask grandparents or elderly neighbours what they used to wash hair, body, clothes and clean teeth when young, and whether these things can be found now (p. 111)
materials: Orange or lemon peel (a few pieces for show-and-tell, if available)
A small neem or babool twig (if locally available, for observation)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of datun and traditional cleaning materials (p. 111)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the story of Moyna and her Dadu from Textbook p. 111, pausing to let children react. Ask: 'Has anyone at home ever mentioned cleaning teeth with a twig or branch?' Let children share freely.

Children open Textbook p. 111 and look at the find-out task. In pairs, they draft three questions they would like to ask an elder — about what the elder used for teeth, hair, body and clothes when young. They write these questions in their notebooks.

Teacher leads a class discussion collecting likely elder answers — datun from neem or babool, reetha for hair, shikakai for body — and writes the names on the board. If a twig or peel sample is present, children observe it closely. Teacher connects this to the eco-cleaner recipe on Textbook p. 112 and explains the two-week process of peels, cloves, and vinegar, asking children what they notice about the ingredients.

Children note the eco-cleaner ingredients and steps in their notebooks as a brief record. Whole-class reflection: 'Why might people today be returning to these older cleaning methods?' Teacher affirms both traditional knowledge and its continuing relevance.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect past everyday practices communicated by elders to present-day alternatives, identifying continuity and change in resource use.
periods.section_context: Datun from neem, karanj, babool twigs; reetha and shikakai as traditional cleaning substances; elder-interview questions about hair, body, clothes and teeth cleaning; eco-friendly home-cleaner using orange or lemon peels, cloves, bay leaves, white vinegar.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt children to think about whether any elder at home still uses these materials: 'Can these things be found now near your home?' This surfaces regional variation in availability and keeps traditional knowledge as lived, not merely historical.

periods.activity_title: Move Like an Animal — Play is Exercise
periods.textbook_anchor: Playing Outdoors and Indoors too — Hop, skip, jump: walk like a duck, jump like a frog, run like a cat, skip with a rope counting jumps, invite a friend to join after 10 skips or a short poem (p. 114)
materials: Notebook and pencil for recording observations

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks children to place one hand on their chest and feel their heartbeat for a moment. Ask: 'What do you think will happen to your heartbeat after you run around?' Record predictions on the board — faster, the same, slower.

The class moves to an open space. Following Textbook p. 114, children try each animal move in sequence: walk like a duck, jump like a frog, run like a cat. After the moves, one or two children use the skipping rope and count jumps aloud; others join after 10 skips or after a short spoken rhyme as described in the textbook.

Children return to their seats and immediately check their breathing and cheeks. Each child writes two or three observations in their notebook: 'My breathing is now… My cheeks feel… My heart feels…' Compare with their earlier prediction on the board.

Teacher connects their observations to the textbook explanation of how exercise makes the heart work harder and the body stronger. Brief discussion: 'How is this kind of play different from watching TV or playing on a phone?' Children share.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record physical changes in their own body caused by exercise and connect those changes to how physical activity strengthens the body.
periods.section_context: Duck walk, frog jump, cat run movements; skipping rope with count and partner-join; faster breathing, red cheeks, sweating as exercise effects; heart working harder making the body stronger.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Draw out the traditional games angle naturally: 'Has anyone played kabaddi or kho-kho? Are those games more tiring or less tiring than skipping — and why?' This connects physical observations to the cultural game knowledge the section develops.

periods.activity_title: Safe Place or Not? — Stranger Safety Roleplay
periods.textbook_anchor: Playing Safely — Identify games shown and whether you have played them before (p. 115)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of five play environments — busy road, park, schoolground, rooftop without railings, construction site (p. 115–116)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 115 and look at the five play-environment illustrations. In pairs, each child decides quickly — safe or unsafe — and shares one reason. Teacher collects responses on the board as a tally without declaring answers yet.

Whole-class discussion of the five environments. For each one, children explain their reasoning: what makes a busy road unsafe, what makes a park safer, why a rooftop without railings is dangerous. Teacher adds the construction-site and stranger-danger contexts from the section, inviting children to explain each in their own words.

Children choose one of the three stranger-dialogue scenarios from the textbook — refusing sweets, refusing to be picked up, refusing a car lift — and act it out in pairs, with one child as the stranger and one as the child saying no. The class watches two or three pairs and briefly discusses: 'What words did they use that made them feel safe?'
Each child writes one rule for playing safely in their notebook — their own words, drawn from the discussion. Teacher reads two or three aloud to close, affirming that these rules protect everyone.

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate familiar play environments for safety and demonstrate appropriate refusal responses to unsafe stranger interactions.
periods.section_context: Five play environments: busy road, park, schoolground, rooftop without railings, construction site; stranger-danger scenarios: refusing sweets, refusing to be picked up, refusing a car lift; paying attention to surroundings.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What would you say to a friend who was about to play near a construction site?' This moves from recognising danger to articulating the protective reasoning — the civic self-protection habit the section develops.

periods.activity_title: Name the Game — Traditional Games Word Search and Discussion
periods.textbook_anchor: Playing Safely — Find names of all games hidden in the word search; identify favourites (p. 116)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook word-search grid and game illustrations (p. 116)

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the idea of indoor and outdoor games from the section. Children look at Textbook p. 116 and note that one game name has already been circled as an example. They predict how many game names are hidden before searching.

Children work individually to find and circle all game names in the Textbook p. 116 word-search using coloured pencils. They write each name they find in their notebook. The teacher circulates and prompts children who are stuck by naming the game aloud for them to locate.

Whole-class sharing: children call out the names they found. Teacher writes them on the board. For each traditional game (spinning top, kabaddi, kho-kho, carrom, etc.), teacher asks: 'Has anyone played this? Where? Who taught you?' Children share short stories about who introduced them to the game.

Each child chooses one game from the list and draws a quick sketch of how it is played, labelling the key object or movement. Teacher closes by connecting: 'These games have been played for generations — someone in your family likely played the same game when they were your age.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe traditional and contemporary games from their cultural environment and connect those games to their own lived experience.
periods.section_context: Word-search game names: kabaddi, kho-kho, cricket, football, badminton, hockey, spinning top, ludo, snakes-and-ladders, carrom; game illustrations; children teaching each other games.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite children to name a game their grandparent or older relative taught them that is not in the word search — this naturally surfaces regional game traditions and keeps cultural diversity central rather than incidental.

periods.activity_title: My Health Portrait — Weekly Table and Day Circle
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw a big circle divided into 24 slices and colour slices by activity for one full day (p. 120)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook weekly health table template and 24-slice circle diagram (p. 119–120)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the unit by connecting all the chapter's themes: body hygiene, traditional cleaning knowledge, the physical effects of exercise, safety in play, and the cultural richness of games. Children briefly name one idea from each theme — no writing yet, just a quick oral sweep across the chapter's content.

Children open Textbook p. 119 and set up the weekly health tracking table in their notebooks — copying the column headings: brushing twice, morning toilet, shower, sleep hours, breakfast, screen time, outdoor play, how I felt. They fill in today's row from memory as honestly as possible.

Children open Textbook p. 120 and draw a large circle, divide it into 24 equal slices using a ruler, and colour the slices according to how they actually spent yesterday — sleep, school, play, meals, screen time, hygiene routines. They label each colour in a small key beside the circle.

Children look at their completed circle and the health table row together. Each child writes one sentence: 'One thing I want to change about my day is…' Teacher asks two or three children to share, then closes by affirming that noticing and choosing are the first steps to staying healthy and happy — the chapter's own message.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent their own daily health habits in structured written and diagrammatic forms and reflect on what those representations reveal about their choices.
periods.section_context: Weekly health tracking table: brushing twice, morning toilet use, shower, sleep hours, breakfast, screen time, outdoor play, how I felt; 24-slice circle diagram coloured by activity type for one full day.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you coloured the circle for a day you played outside a lot, how would it look different from a day you spent mostly indoors with a screen?' This connects the visual representation back to the chapter's core argument that balance across hygiene, exercise and rest keeps the body and mind healthy.

assessment_items.task: Look at the list below. Put a tick next to every habit you actually did yesterday. Then circle ONE habit you would like to do more carefully from tomorrow. Write one sentence saying why that habit matters for your health.
assessment_items.scaffold: Habits: Take a shower / Wash hands with soap after toilet / Brush teeth in the morning / Brush teeth at night / Drink 6–8 glasses of water / Eat breakfast / Sleep for at least 8 hours / Play outdoors. My circled habit: ___________. Why it matters: ___________.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any honestly completed checklist. The quality of the item lies in the reasoning sentence: does the child connect the habit to a health outcome (body stays clean, disease is prevented, body gets stronger)? There is no single correct habit to circle.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can audit their own daily habits against a health checklist and identify areas for personal improvement.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can match real daily behaviour against a health-hygiene checklist and articulate why a specific habit protects the body — moving from self-audit to health reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The checklist grounds the task in the section's own list; the circled habit prompts selection; the written sentence reveals whether the child understands the health reason, not just the habit name.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: checklist reflects honest recall; circled habit is clearly named; sentence connects habit to a body or health outcome (e.g., 'If I brush at night, food bits don't hurt my teeth'). Weak: all items ticked without discrimination; sentence merely repeats the habit name without a health reason.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children with limited writing ability may dictate their sentence to the teacher or draw an arrow from the habit to a picture of a healthy body part. Children who do not shower daily due to water access concerns should not be penalised — the focus is reasoning, not compliance.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The checklist mirrors the section's own self-check structure, making the task directly continuous with the activity; the sentence shifts cognitive demand from recall to evaluation.

assessment_items.question_text: Moyna's Dadu told her that he used a neem twig called a datun to clean his teeth when he was young. Name ONE other traditional material elders used for cleaning the body or hair, and explain ONE reason why people today might choose to use these traditional materials again.
expected_elements: Names at least one traditional cleaning material other than datun — reetha or shikakai are the expected responses from the section.

Gives one reason for returning to traditional materials — e.g., they are natural and do not harm the environment, they are eco-friendly, they have been used safely for a long time, or similar reasoning grounded in the section.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept reetha, shikakai, or any other plant-based material the child may have heard about from an elder, provided the reason is grounded in natural or eco-friendly properties. Regional variation note: elders in different parts of India may have used different plant materials (e.g., triphala, aritha) — regionally varied material names are acceptable and correct provided the child names something from traditional practice.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How do we Brush our Teeth?
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect past everyday practices communicated by elders to present-day alternatives, identifying continuity and change in resource use.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

expected_elements: Names at least one traditional cleaning material (reetha, shikakai, or a locally known equivalent) for body or hair cleaning.
Provides a reason for returning to traditional materials that reflects the eco-friendly or natural-substance logic of the section — not merely 'elders said so'.

assessment_items.question_text: After Priya ran around the playground doing the frog-jump and cat-run, she noticed her cheeks were red and she was breathing fast. What is the BEST explanation for these changes in her body?

options.label: A
options.text: Her heart was working harder to pump blood, making her body stronger.

options.label: B
options.text: Priya was sick and had a fever from being outside.

options.label: C
options.text: She was embarrassed because her friends were watching her.

options.label: D
options.text: The sun was too hot and she needed to drink water immediately.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This item checks whether the child can attribute visible bodily changes to exercise physiology as explained in the section, not to unrelated causes.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record physical changes in their own body caused by exercise and connect those changes to how physical activity strengthens the body.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'sick and had a fever' shows the child confuses the normal effects of exercise with symptoms of illness — a misconception between healthy physical exertion and disease.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'sun was too hot' shows the child attributes the changes to an external environmental factor rather than to the body's own internal response to movement.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'embarrassed' shows the child assigns a social-emotional cause to a physical change, conflating emotional blushing with exercise-induced circulation.

assessment_items.question_text: Rajan wants to go and play near a construction site because his friends are already there. Write what you would say to Rajan to explain why that place is not safe for playing, and suggest one safer place where they could play instead.
look_for: Identifies at least one specific danger at a construction site — falling materials, open pits, heavy machinery, no adult supervision — rather than a vague 'it is dangerous'.
Gives reasoning that connects the danger to a possible harm to a child — e.g., something could fall on them, there are no safety barriers, children are not allowed there.
Suggests a genuinely safer alternative play space — a park, schoolground, or open ground — with at least a brief reason why it is safer.
Uses a persuasive tone addressed to Rajan rather than writing a general essay about safety.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: the safer alternative suggested may vary — an open courtyard, a temple ground, a community field — all are acceptable if the child explains why it is safer. Award marks for quality of reasoning, not for naming a specific place.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate familiar play environments for safety and demonstrate appropriate refusal responses to unsafe stranger interactions.

competency.competency_text: Develops simple labels and slogans, and participates in roleplay on safety and protection in the local environment to be displayed/done in school and locality

look_for: Names a specific hazard at the construction site — not just 'it is bad' but what exactly could cause harm.
Explains how that hazard connects to injury or danger for a child playing there.
Proposes an alternative play space and gives at least one reason it is safer (adults present, open space, no heavy materials, known environment).
Addresses Rajan directly — the item asks for persuasion, and a response that reads as a list of facts rather than a message to a friend is weaker.

assessment_items.question_text: Kabaddi, kho-kho, and spinning tops are traditional games that have been played in India for a very long time. What does playing and sharing these games with friends BEST help us do?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the body healthy by using the latest sports equipment.

options.label: B
options.text: Pass on cultural traditions and stay active at the same time.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace screen time only when there is no electricity at home.

options.label: D
options.text: Win prizes and trophies at school sports competitions.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: C. This item checks whether the child recognises that traditional games serve both a cultural-transmission function and a physical health function, as the section presents them.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe traditional and contemporary games from their cultural environment and connect those games to their own lived experience.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'win prizes' shows the child associates games only with competition outcomes rather than with cultural identity or health — a confusion between competitive sport and traditional play.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'latest sports equipment' shows the child conflates modern sporting goods with traditional games, not grasping that traditional games are valued precisely because they do not require special equipment.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'replace screen time only when no electricity' shows the child treats traditional games as a fallback rather than as a culturally valuable and physically healthy activity in their own right.

assessment_items.task: Draw a large circle in your notebook and divide it into 24 equal slices — each slice stands for one hour of a full day. Colour the slices to show how you spent yesterday. Use a different colour for each type of activity: sleeping, school, outdoor play, meals, hygiene routines, screen time, and anything else you did. Make a small colour key beside the circle.
assessment_items.scaffold: Colour key: Sleep = ___ / School = ___ / Outdoor play = ___ / Meals = ___ / Hygiene (brush, shower, etc.) = ___ / Screen time = ___ / Other = ___. After colouring, write ONE sentence: 'I noticed that I spent the most time on ___________ and the least time on ___________.'
assessment_items.annotation: There is no single correct circle — each child's day is different. Assess whether the circle accounts for roughly 24 hours, whether the colour key matches the colouring, and whether the observation sentence reflects what the diagram actually shows. Regional variation note: activities such as helping at home, fetching water, or attending religious practice are valid time uses and should be included without judgement.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent their own daily health habits in structured written and diagrammatic forms and reflect on what those representations reveal about their choices.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can translate lived time-use into a proportional visual representation and extract a simple observation from that representation — combining diagrammatic expression with self-reflection.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The colour key ensures the diagram is readable and the child has named their categories. The observation sentence checks that the child reads their own diagram rather than just producing a colourful circle.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: slices plausibly add to 24 hours; colours match the key consistently; observation sentence names specific activities and compares them. Weak: random colouring with no key; observation sentence is generic ('I slept') without using the diagram's proportions.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find dividing a circle difficult may draw 24 small squares in a row instead — the proportional logic is the same. Children may name activity categories in their home language in the key.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Diagram with key and written sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The 24-slice circle is the section's own task format; it simultaneously develops proportional thinking and health self-awareness, making it the most direct expression of the implied_lo.
